outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the Euclidean statement (for all n, linear independence of Atiyah's n polynomials, equivalently non-singularity of the n-by-n matrix) has been claimed false in three 2026 items: a 46-point helix counterexample with a Lean 4 formalisation proposed as an open, unmerged GitHub PR to google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (8 Oct 2026, approved by a repository reviewer on 11 Oct 2026); a Zenodo preprint by Jan Eickhoff claiming arbitrarily large dependent configurations (8 Sep 2026, later version 28 Sep 2026); and a Zenodo preprint by Hu Tan and Ying Zhang claiming a 24-point dependent configuration (22 Sep 2026); the same authors' 4 Oct 2026 preprint claims the statement holds at n = 5. No journal-refereed result on general n has appeared in the window, and no human mathematician outside the PR review has publicly engaged with any of the 2026 Euclidean claims.
problem_asks: Unpacked from the bullet's statement ('on the invertibility of a certain n-by-n matrix depending on n points in R3'): (a) for every n (the claim is over all n, not a single n); (b) for every configuration of n points in Euclidean three-space (the bullet says 'n points' without 'distinct'; Atiyah's construction, the literature and the formal-conjectures statement all require distinct points, so distinctness is taken as the hypothesis); (c) the n-by-n matrix built from the configuration is non-singular (invertible). In the literature the matrix is the coefficient matrix of the n polynomials p_1..p_n, where p_i has as roots the stereographic images of the unit directions from x_i to the other points, so (c) is equivalent to linear independence over C of the p_i (Atiyah's Conjecture 1). The bullet does not name the stronger Atiyah–Sutcliffe Conjecture 2 (|D| at least 1, with D the normalised determinant) or Conjecture 3 (the deletion inequality); those are related but are not asked by the bullet's words. The fetched Wikipedia article describes the matrix only as 'a certain n by n matrix' (a fetch summary reports a 'which?' tag on that phrase). Known before the window: n = 1, 2 trivially; n = 3 (Atiyah); n = 4 (Eastwood and Norbury); some special families (Đoković; Svrtan and Urbiha).

events.what_happened: Atiyah's own n = 3 case of the non-vanishing / linear independence statement, given as a geometric argument and an algebraic argument in Atiyah's 2000 Surveys in Differential Geometry paper 'The geometry of classical particles' and his 2001 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A paper 'Configurations of points'. Dated to the year only. NOT OPENED: this comes from the Wikipedia article's reference list (a fetch of the article reports Atiyah 2000 and Atiyah 2001 as the sources that introduced the conjecture) and from search summaries, which say the n = 3 case is proved in those papers. I did not verify that the n = 3 argument appears in them.
events.delivers: Non-singularity (linear independence of the three polynomials) for every three distinct points in Euclidean R3, i.e. the statement for n = 3. Per search summaries only.
events.remains: All n >= 4 for the general statement.
events.directly_checkable: The n = 3 case is elementary and can be checked by hand from the definition, but I did not check the paper's argument.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture (non-singularity) for n = 3.

events.what_happened: Malkoun, 'Finite graphs and configurations of points', arXiv 2508.13472 (v1 19 Aug 2025; v2 9 Mar 2026; v3 7 Sep 2026, the version read). Generalises the Atiyah configuration problem and the Atiyah–Sutcliffe Conjectures 1 and 2 from the complete graph to arbitrary finite graphs, replacing the determinant with a 'G-amplitude function'. States Conjectures A, B, C, D as its own geometric inequalities (unproven in general) and proves restricted theorems: Theorem 4.1 (Conjecture D implies Conjecture C), Proposition 4.3 (Conjecture C for star graphs), and Theorem 4.4 (Conjecture C for linear graphs with 2 <= n <= 5). The paper says that for the complete graph, Conjecture B is equivalent to AS Conjecture 2 and is known in general only for n <= 4, and that Conjectures 1 and 2 have been proved for n <= 4 citing other work. Acknowledges 'the anonymous reviewer', so a referee process is implied; the journal is not named on the page.
events.revisions: v1 19 Aug 2025; v2 9 Mar 2026; v3 7 Sep 2026 (read).
events.delivers: Generalisation to finite graphs with conjectures; restricted theorems about graph amplitudes for star graphs and linear graphs with at most five vertices, and an implication from Conjecture D to Conjecture C. None of these is the Euclidean statement for general n. Its own ChatGPT-assisted step is a proof of Conjecture B for the linear graph with n = 5 (see ai).
events.remains: Conjecture 1 and Conjecture 2 of Atiyah–Sutcliffe for n >= 5 in R3; Conjectures A, B, C, D for general graphs.
events.directly_checkable: The linear and star graph cases are finite computations in principle; the paper uses Julia Symbolics for an algebraic step (per a summarising fetch).
events.doubts: Conjectural framework; the author says the ChatGPT-assisted step is part of a proof for linear graph with n = 5 rather than for the Euclidean problem. No public commentary found.
events.direction: Generalisation; none of its results is the Euclidean statement at any n, and it states that Atiyah Conjectures 1 and 2 are proved for n <= 4 only (citing other work).

events.what_happened: Ziran Liu, 'Atiyah's Minkowski Space Conjecture Fails for Every n >= 3', arXiv 2608.16693 (v1 only, 17 Aug 2026; math.DG, cross-listed math-ph and math.MG; affiliations SIMIS and Fudan Research Institute of Intelligent Complex Systems per the HTML). It disproves Atiyah's Minkowski-space conjecture (linear independence of binary forms attached to n worldlines) for every n >= 3: for n = 3 an explicit planar one-parameter family of worldlines whose coefficient determinant has one simple zero, with coefficient matrix of rank exactly two; for n > 3 a null-translation extension. The paper's own text says the Euclidean linear-independence conjecture is elementary for n <= 3 and that 'the present counterexamples do not address either of those separate conjectures', and that they 'do not contradict the Euclidean or hyperbolic results just reviewed'.
events.delivers: Minkowski-space analogue only: linear dependence for every n >= 3 in Minkowski spacetime, with explicit counterexamples. The paper says it does not address the Euclidean R3 conjecture.
events.remains: Euclidean R3 Conjecture 1 for every n, Conjectures 2 and 3, and the hyperbolic version, all untouched by this paper.
events.directly_checkable: The n = 3 counterexample is an explicit planar family of three worldlines with marked events and a parameter T; checkable by a computation the paper describes (Proposition 5.1 is proved in Appendix A by exact rational interval estimates).
events.doubts: Single unrefereed arXiv version; no independent check or response found. The paper's Proposition 5.1 depends on rational interval estimates in Appendix A; whether they were done by hand or by computer is not stated in the portion I read.
events.direction: Cuts against the Minkowski analogue; no direction on the Euclidean statement, which the paper explicitly leaves alone.
events.object: For n = 3: an explicit planar one-parameter family of three complete affine worldlines with marked events, such that the coefficient determinant has exactly one simple zero in a specified interval and the coefficient matrix has rank exactly two (linear dependence). For n > 3: a null-translation construction that multiplies the first three forms by a common factor. Both explicit, not existence proofs. Minkowski space, not R3.

events.what_happened: Hu Tan and Ying Zhang, 'A 24-Point Atiyah Singular Configuration', Zenodo preprint 10.5281/zenodo.22904483, published 22 Sep 2026 (CC BY 4.0). Record abstract: an explicit set of '24 distinct, noncoplanar points in Euclidean 3-space' belonging to a reflection-symmetric one-parameter family given by an integer coordinate table; the normalised Atiyah–Sutcliffe determinant has a unique simple zero in a rational interval of length 10^-20, where the 24-by-24 coefficient matrix has rank exactly 23; the proof combines an exact real-matrix reduction with certified endpoint and derivative bounds from outward interval arithmetic in integers. The PDF (388 kB) was not readable through my tools; the coordinates are not in the landing page.
events.revisions: v1 (record revision 4 on Zenodo; concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22904482); no later version found.
events.delivers: Claims that the Atiyah polynomials of this explicit 24-point configuration are linearly dependent, so the matrix is singular at n = 24: a counterexample to Conjecture 1 at n = 24 only. Because the normalised determinant vanishes there, the record's zero also means |D| is less than 1 at that configuration (an inference of mine), which would contradict Conjecture 2 as well.
events.remains: All other n; Conjectures 2 and 3 are not claimed beyond the configuration itself.
events.directly_checkable: The integer coordinate table and the zero interval are in the PDF, which I could not read. Checkable by high-precision recomputation of the 24-by-24 coefficient determinant or rank at the stated parameter.
events.doubts: Single Zenodo preprint; correctness rests on the interval certification, and no code repository is named in the record. The zero is located to width 10^-20 and the claim turns on that certificate. Authors: Hu Tan (Chinese Academy of Sciences) and Ying Zhang (Soochow University); Ying Zhang appears in a 2019 Malkoun citation as co-author with J. Ma of a hyperbolic four-point result, so the author is not wholly outside the field. No review or public engagement found.
events.direction: Cuts against Conjecture 1 at n = 24 (and, by the record's own zero of the normalised determinant, against Conjecture 2 at that configuration).
events.object: An explicit 24-point noncoplanar configuration in Euclidean R3, from a reflection-symmetric one-parameter family given by an integer coordinate table, at whose parameter the normalised Atiyah–Sutcliffe determinant has a unique simple zero (located in an interval of width 10^-20 by certified bounds). At that zero the coefficient matrix has rank 23, so the Atiyah polynomials are linearly dependent. The family is explicit; the zero is located by certified numerics rather than a closed form.

events.what_happened: Hu Tan and Ying Zhang, 'The Atiyah-Sutcliffe determinant at five points: positivity and failure of the deletion inequality', Zenodo preprint 10.5281/zenodo.23142909, published 4 Oct 2026 (CC BY 4.0; with a code archive, 57 kB). Record abstract: for every five-point configuration in Euclidean 3-space 'the real part of the determinant is at least 5/768, proving Atiyah's conjecture in this cardinality'; an explicit planar integer-coordinate five-point configuration violates the stronger deletion inequality while its determinant and all five deletion determinants exceed one; five is the smallest cardinality where this can happen; and adjoining sufficiently distant points gives planar integer counterexamples to the deletion inequality in every larger cardinality. The positivity proof uses a polarised determinant, signed-volume inequalities and an exact cut-variable certificate; the counterexample is certified by rational interval arithmetic. The PDF (148 kB) and code were not read.
events.delivers: Claims Conjecture 1 (non-vanishing / linear independence) for n = 5 in Euclidean R3, by a positivity bound on the real part of the determinant. Separately claims a failure of the deletion inequality (a stronger Atiyah–Sutcliffe inequality, not Conjecture 1 or 2) for planar configurations of n >= 5. The record's |D| > 1 at the planar counterexample is consistent with Conjecture 2 holding there.
events.remains: Conjecture 1 for n >= 6; Conjecture 2 for n >= 6 and in general; the deletion inequality outside the planar counterexamples (not asked by the bullet).
events.directly_checkable: The five-point bound is a finite algebraic inequality over the configuration space that could be checked from the code archive (not read). The planar integer counterexample can be checked by exact arithmetic from its coordinates (not read).
events.doubts: Single Zenodo preprint, same authors as the 24-point record; no review; the code archive and PDF were not read. Consistent with the 46-point PR (which does not exclude n = 5), and with the 24-point claim, though these are different n.
events.direction: For n = 5: cuts toward Conjecture 1 holding. For the deletion inequality (not the bullet's quantity): cuts against it at n >= 5 in the planar integer examples.
events.object: A planar integer-coordinate five-point configuration in Euclidean R3 violating the stronger deletion inequality, with |D| and all five deletion determinants exceeding one (coordinates not read). The positivity result is a bound, not an object.

events.what_happened: GitHub user azakhtyamov opened issue #6965 and pull request #6966 on google-deepmind/formal-conjectures on 8 Oct 2026, titled 'Atiyah–Sutcliffe Conjecture 1 is false: mark conjecture_one solved, add conjecture_one_false'. The PR changes FormalConjectures/Arxiv/1102.4662/AtiyahSutcliffe.lean: conjecture_one is re-annotated from research open to research solved and restated as an answer(False) iff form, and a new conjecture_one_false is added. The PR description says: 'AtiyahSutcliffe.conjecture_one is refuted by an explicit injective configuration of 46 points in R3'; 'These are 46 equally spaced points on a circular helix of radius 1 whose axis is the y-axis'; the points are (sin t theta, t b, cos t theta) for odd t in -45..45, with theta and b given to about 75 digits; the pair t = +-35 is moved by at most 10^-40 onto a zero of a Schur residual; the zero is established by 'a Newton–Kantorovich argument evaluated in rigorous interval arithmetic' in 320-bit intervals, which the Lean kernel re-evaluates; the proof is a single Lean file in the external repository azakhtyamov/atiyah-sutcliffe-disproof (AtiyahSutcliffeDisproof.lean, about 4,195 lines), built on Lean 4.33.1 and Mathlib v4.33.1; the PR's axioms are propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The PR says 'There is no conceptual explanation of why this helix is singular; the zero was found by computer search.' The PR also gives a provenance line (see ai). Status at the time of reading: PR open, not merged; a reviewer requested changes on 10 Oct and approved on 11 Oct 2026 after an independent re-check.
events.revisions: Issue and PR opened 8 Oct 2026. Branch force-pushed 8 Oct 2026 (c87b868 to 49a99ed). Commit bed91f1 'Point the formal_proof links at the renamed proof' on 10 Oct 2026. Reviewer requested changes 10 Oct; author replied 10 Oct (proof renamed to AtiyahSutcliffeDisproof.conjecture_one_false; links pinned to commit 6d83789 in the external repo; verify.sh no longer masks errors); approval 11 Oct 2026. External repo: master branch, 5 commits.
events.delivers: Claims that the Lean statement AtiyahSutcliffe.conjecture_one (for every n and every injective x : Fin n -> R3, the point polynomials are linearly independent over C) is false, via an injective 46-point configuration with a certified zero. Per the PR this is the statement of Conjecture 1 as formalised in the repository (the repository docstring calls it 'The first Atiyah–Sutcliffe conjecture'). It establishes the failure of the universal statement for n = 46 only. The PR says the smallest counterexample size is not known; one search-result summary of the PR says it lies between 5 and 46, which my direct fetch did not confirm.
events.remains: Conjectures 2 and 3 are not addressed. Whether counterexamples exist for smaller n is not addressed by the PR. The PR is not merged.

events.directly_checkable: The configuration is given by a formula with explicit parameters: the external README gives points (sin((2j+1)theta), (2j+1)b, cos((2j+1)theta)) for j = 0..22 with their images under (x, y, z) -> (-x, -y, z); tan(theta/2) = twistNum/10^76 and b = riseNum/10^75 (the fetched README renders the exponents as 1076 and 1075). Checking the determinant or rank of the 46-point coefficient matrix at these parameters needs high-precision computation, not hand arithmetic. The Lean file is the checkable object.
events.doubts: (i) The PR is open and not merged; the reviewer's independent check is reported in a comment and not in a log I read. (ii) The witness was found by computer search, and the PR states there is no conceptual explanation of the singularity. (iii) The proof lives in a separate repository by one author with no stars, no license shown, and five commits; I read only about 1,000 of 4,195 lines of its Lean file, with no sorry or native_decide among the lines read. (iv) The interval arithmetic is a custom 320-bit fixed-point development (README), not a standard library, certified by re-evaluation in the kernel. (v) In the formal-conjectures file, conjecture_one and conjecture_one_false end in sorry as proof placeholders with formal_proof links to the external file; that is the repository's usual pattern (my reading), so the sorry-free status depends on the external file. (vi) Citation inconsistency: the repository docstring cites 'Conjecture 1.1' in Mazur–Petrenko, while the reviewer says the statement 'matches the published Conjecture 2.1'. Not resolved, because I did not read Mazur–Petrenko's full text. (vii) The formal statement quantifies over injective configurations, i.e. distinct points, which matches the literature's hypothesis.
events.direction: Cuts against Conjecture 1 as formalised: the claim is that the 46 point polynomials are linearly dependent for an injective configuration, so the universal statement fails. If the zero is genuine, the normalised determinant vanishes there, which would also violate Conjecture 2 at that configuration (my inference; the PR does not say so).
events.object: An injective configuration of 46 points in R3: the points (sin t theta, t b, cos t theta) for odd t from -45 to 45, i.e. 46 equally spaced points on a unit-radius helix about the y-axis, with theta ~ 0.1369716 and b ~ 0.3018996 (given to about 75 digits in the repository), and the points t = +-35 displaced by at most 10^-40 onto a zero of a Schur residual found by computer search. The zero is certified by a Newton–Kantorovich argument in interval arithmetic. The configuration is explicit up to that certified perturbation. It shows the 46 point polynomials are linearly dependent.

summary: The bullet asks whether, for every n, the n-by-n matrix built from n points of Euclidean R3 is non-singular, equivalently whether Atiyah's n polynomials are always linearly independent (Atiyah's Conjecture 1). Before the window: n = 3 is attributed to Atiyah (2000/2001, not opened); n = 4 is proved by Eastwood and Norbury (2001, Geom. Topol.) and re-proved by Malkoun (2022); special families by Đoković (2002) and Svrtan and Urbiha (2004/2006, which also state C1 as proved for n = 3, 4 and special families only); the stronger conjectures C2/C3 have planar and four-point results (Mazur and Petrenko 2011; Bou Khuzam 2021; Bou Khuzam and Johnson 2014, computer-aided with Maple; Svrtan's 2014 four-point claim, known only from a search summary). In the window, the only refereed or journal-track items are Guerra–Salvatore (Oct 2024, conditional on the strong Atiyah–Sutcliffe conjecture, no AI named in the full text) and Malkoun (Aug 2025, v3 Sep 2026, a graph-amplitude generalisation with restricted theorems; it names ChatGPT version 5.3 for part of a proof of Conjecture B for a linear graph with n = 5, which is not the Euclidean statement). Two in-window items are analogues and do not bear on the Euclidean statement: Liu (17 Aug 2026) disproves the Minkowski-space version for every n >= 3 and says in its own text that the Euclidean case is untouched; Lyu, Ma, Tan and Zhang (6 Oct 2026) claim a complete four-point hyperbolic proof and an error in Malkoun's published hyperbolic proof. The Euclidean in-window claims are: Eickhoff (Zenodo, 8 Sep 2026; later record 28 Sep 2026) claiming dependent configurations for arbitrarily large n, with the later version adding planar and hyperbolic claims; Tan and Zhang (Zenodo, 22 Sep 2026) claiming an explicit 24-point configuration with a certified zero of the normalised determinant and rank 23 (computer-assisted); Tan and Zhang (Zenodo, 4 Oct 2026) claiming Re det at least 5/768 for every five-point configuration, which proves C1 at n = 5, plus planar deletion-inequality counterexamples; and the GitHub PR #6966 (8 Oct 2026, open and unmerged, approved by a reviewer on 11 Oct) which formalises a 46-point helix counterexample to Conjecture 1 in Lean 4.33.1 with an interval certificate kept in an external repository. I read the Zenodo landing pages and metadata only, because the PDFs could not be read with my tools; the mathematics of the three Zenodo items is therefore unverified by me. The PR's own description attributes the work to a 'researching model' (ChatGPT Astra, gpt-6-astra) and a reviewer (Claude Fable 5.1) and says the witness was found by computer search inside an autoresearch loop; that is the only AI attribution for the Euclidean claims. The Lean file's sorry-free status rests on the author's and reviewer's statements plus about a quarter of the file that I read. Close calls: (a) whether the PR's reviewer check counts as a qualified human check depends on a reviewer identity I could not establish; (b) whether the AI involvement is load-bearing depends on what the 'researching model' did in the loop, which the PR does not spell out; (c) the Tan and Zhang five-point claim and the PR do not contradict each other, since the PR does not claim a counterexample at n = 5. No journal or human expert write-up of any Euclidean claim was found in the window. The problem has no article-level status change on Wikipedia that I could see; the cached article I read was last edited November 2022 and is a stub on this point.
competing_reading: The strongest case that the Euclidean statement is now settled negatively: a formal Lean 4 counterexample at n = 46 with an interval certificate, checked by a second party (the reviewer reports an independent rebuild with the three standard axioms), and two further independent constructions at other n by different authors (Eickhoff for arbitrarily large n; Tan and Zhang for n = 24), all in the same two-month window. Against that: none of the constructions has been published in a refereed venue, the Lean proof is in an unmerged PR and a separate repository, the witness came from a computer search with no conceptual explanation, the Zenodo papers were not reviewed, and the only checker of the Lean file is a reviewer whose standing is not established. On the strict reading the problem is 'claimed false, unrefereed' on 11 October 2026, and the Tan and Zhang five-point claim (not contradicting the PR) would, if correct, push any counterexample to n >= 6.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Merge of PR #6966, or an independent full-file build of AtiyahSutcliffeDisproof.lean at the pinned commits with confirmed absence of sorry and native_decide (the repo logs are listed but not read). (2) An independent high-precision computation of the 46-point coefficient matrix determinant or rank at the stated parameters (twistNum/10^76, riseNum/10^75). (3) Reading the two Eickhoff PDFs and the Tan and Zhang 24-point PDF: explicit construction, which n, and how linear dependence is verified; the five-point PDF and code for the n = 5 bound. (4) A refereed publication or an expert write-up of any of these. (5) Resolution of the reviewer's 'Conjecture 2.1' against the docstring's 'Conjecture 1.1' in Mazur–Petrenko, to confirm the Lean statement is the one the literature calls Conjecture 1. (6) The PR's loop logs or a provenance note saying what ChatGPT Astra (gpt-6-astra) and Claude Fable 5.1 each did, and whether the witness search was run by the model or by a separate tool.
